units.title: 1. Team flow and version control
units.description: Small changes, branches, review, merge conflicts, tags, release notes, and collaboration.

lessons.title: Make changes small and reviewable
lessons.summary: Make changes small and reviewable. Learn the key idea, then apply it to a realistic system decision.
notes: Version control records project history so people can compare, review, and recover changes. Small branches and coherent commits help reviewers understand intent. A review request should explain scope, test evidence, and any effect on configuration or operations.

Keep changes focused and avoid including unrelated generated files or secrets. A branch is not a substitute for review, and merging is not proof of correctness. Make rollback or forward-fix options clear when a change affects a running service.

quiz.question: Why split a large change into focused commits or reviews?
options: It makes intent, impact, and test evidence easier to understand.
It prevents reviewers from noticing unrelated changes.
Assume the system behavior without checking it.
quiz.explanation: It makes intent, impact, and test evidence easier to understand. Confirm it with relevant evidence and state any limits.

practice.title: Team flow and version control

options: Choose the fastest action without checking impact.

practice.explanation: A description of the change, verification, and rollback plan. This keeps the work scoped and reviewable.

lessons.title: Use Git history to coordinate and recover
lessons.summary: Use Git history to coordinate and recover. Learn the key idea, then apply it to a realistic system decision.
notes: A build artifact is the output produced from source and dependencies. Identifying it by a version or digest lets teams connect a deployed result to its source revision and checks. Provenance records how the artifact was built and what inputs were used.

Promote the same tested artifact through environments instead of rebuilding it differently at each step. Keep build logs useful but free of secrets. When an issue appears, trace the deployment back to its source and dependencies before attempting a fix.

units.title: 2. Builds and continuous integration
units.description: Build automation, tests, artifacts, pipeline triggers, secrets handling, and feedback loops.

lessons.title: Build and test every proposed change
lessons.summary: Build and test every proposed change. Learn the key idea, then apply it to a realistic system decision.
notes: Continuous integration runs repeatable checks when changes are proposed or combined. Builds, unit checks, formatting, and dependency analysis can give fast feedback. The checks should be maintained and specific enough that a passing result communicates something meaningful.

A green pipeline means only that configured checks passed; it does not prove every behavior is correct or secure. Keep tests deterministic and make failures easy to diagnose. Fix flaky checks rather than rerunning until one happens to pass.

quiz.question: What should happen to a tested build artifact before deployment?
options: Promote the same identified artifact through environments.
Rebuild it differently in production without recording inputs.
Assume the system behavior without checking it.
quiz.explanation: Promote the same identified artifact through environments. Confirm it with relevant evidence and state any limits.

options: Choose the fastest action without checking impact.
Only the narrow permissions needed to publish that preview.
Full organization administrator access.
practice.explanation: Only the narrow permissions needed to publish that preview. This keeps the work scoped and reviewable.

lessons.title: Keep CI permissions and secrets scoped
lessons.summary: Keep CI permissions and secrets scoped. Learn the key idea, then apply it to a realistic system decision.
notes: CI jobs execute code and can reach repositories, registries, or cloud services. Give each job only the permissions it needs. Use short-lived credentials when possible, and protect release or deployment steps with appropriate controls.

External contributions and dependencies may influence workflow execution. Do not expose deployment secrets to untrusted jobs, pin or verify important inputs, and inspect logs for accidental disclosure. If a token leaks, rotate it and investigate its use.

units.title: 3. Containers and application packaging
units.description: Images, containers, registries, configuration, health checks, and safe local container practice.

lessons.title: Package an application into a container image
lessons.summary: Package an application into a container image. Learn the key idea, then apply it to a realistic system decision.
notes: A container image packages an application and its runtime dependencies; a container runs that image with configuration and resource limits. Images can reduce environmental differences, but they do not remove the need to understand base images, ports, filesystem access, and process identity.

Build from trusted sources, keep images focused, and avoid embedding credentials in image layers. Run with the minimum privileges needed. A container that can access the host broadly can undermine the isolation the team expected.

quiz.question: A container image works on one laptop but fails in a clean environment. What is a useful check?
options: Inspect its build inputs, startup command, required configuration, and logs.
Increase host privileges without investigating.
Assume the system behavior without checking it.
quiz.explanation: Inspect its build inputs, startup command, required configuration, and logs. Confirm it with relevant evidence and state any limits.

lessons.title: Configure and run containers safely
lessons.summary: Configure and run containers safely. Learn the key idea, then apply it to a realistic system decision.
notes: Runtime configuration differs across development, test, and production environments. Supply settings at runtime and keep secrets in an appropriate secret store. Health checks should indicate whether the service can do useful work, not simply whether a process exists.

Containers are replaceable, so data that must survive a restart belongs in an explicit persistent storage plan. Send logs where the runtime can collect them, and test startup and shutdown behavior in a clean environment rather than only on the developer’s laptop.

units.title: 4. Deployment and infrastructure as code
units.description: Environments, deployment strategies, rollback, declarative infrastructure, and reviewable changes.

lessons.title: Release changes gradually and plan rollback
lessons.summary: Release changes gradually and plan rollback. Learn the key idea, then apply it to a realistic system decision.
notes: Rolling, canary, and blue-green deployments control how new versions reach users. Gradual exposure can reveal problems before everyone is affected, while a rollback can restore a known-good version when signals cross a defined threshold.

A code rollback may not undo a database migration or external side effect. Design compatible changes and rehearse recovery. Decide who can pause a release and which user-facing signals matter before the deployment begins.

quiz.question: A canary release raises the service error rate. What is the safe next step?
options: Pause or roll back using the release policy, then investigate.
Increase canary traffic to spread the errors faster.
Assume the system behavior without checking it.
quiz.explanation: Pause or roll back using the release policy, then investigate. Confirm it with relevant evidence and state any limits.

lessons.title: Review infrastructure changes before applying them
lessons.summary: Review infrastructure changes before applying them. Learn the key idea, then apply it to a realistic system decision.
notes: Infrastructure as code describes infrastructure changes in files that can be reviewed and versioned. A plan or preview helps show what resources will be created, modified, or removed before applying it. Reusable modules can reduce inconsistency when their inputs and permissions are clear.

Treat infrastructure changes as potentially production-impacting code. Review network exposure, identity scope, data deletion, and cost. Protect state and credentials, and test changes in a safe environment before applying them to shared infrastructure.

units.title: 5. Observability and delivery capstone
units.description: Automate a sample service build, package it, deploy to a local environment, add health checks, and document a rollback plan.

lessons.title: Trace a release from source to running service
lessons.summary: Trace a release from source to running service. Learn the key idea, then apply it to a realistic system decision.
notes: Observability links delivery to runtime behavior. Metrics show trends, logs record events, and traces follow requests across dependencies. A health check, dashboard, and runbook should help an operator decide whether a new release is behaving as expected.

Monitor user outcomes after deployment and compare them with the release policy. A successful pipeline cannot detect every production issue. Make rollback instructions and service ownership easy to find, and review alerts that are noisy or missing.

quiz.question: A deployment command succeeds but users see errors. What is the right signal?
options: User-facing health and error indicators, plus a clear rollback decision.
The command exit code alone.
Assume the system behavior without checking it.
quiz.explanation: User-facing health and error indicators, plus a clear rollback decision. Confirm it with relevant evidence and state any limits.

lessons.title: Demonstrate a safe deployment and recovery path
lessons.summary: Demonstrate a safe deployment and recovery path. Learn the key idea, then apply it to a realistic system decision.
notes: A delivery capstone should trace one change from source review through checks, artifact, deployment, and health signals. Record the source revision and show how to reproduce the build. A runbook should state how to verify the service and restore a known-good state.

Demonstrate the process in a local or otherwise safe environment. Include one failure case, such as a failed health check, and show what the pipeline or operator does. State what the demo does not cover instead of claiming production readiness.
